## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="w9-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Power and energy</dt><dd>A 25 MW, 100 MWh battery charges or discharges at up to 25 MW and holds up to 100 MWh: four hours flat out.</dd>
<dt>Round-trip efficiency</dt><dd>This battery returns 80% of what goes in; the rest becomes heat.</dd>
<dt>State of charge</dt><dd>The energy stored at the end of each hour; it links each hour to the next.</dd>
<dt>Value</dt><dd>The battery's value is what it saves the town: $7,240 on this day with the best schedule.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Prices, losses and the break-even spread</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A MWh stored at a price $p_\text{in}$ comes back as 0.8 MWh. It pays only if the selling price beats $p_\text{in}/0.8$: buy at \$40, and you must sell above \$50. Buying spilled sun at \$0 always passes this test, which is why the best schedule charges at midday.

The [price]{.lx-term term="marginal-cost"} on each hour is the cost of *one more* MWh. A 25 MW battery is not one MWh: at 08:00 only 3 MW of sun is spilled, so charging at full power takes 22 MW from the gas plant at \$40. This lesson therefore counts the town's real saving. The best full-power schedule you can tap saves \$6,360; the solver saves \$7,240 because it charges at part power, exactly what each hour spills.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The battery's day as a linear program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For each hour $t$: charging $c_t$, discharging $d_t$ and the [state of charge]{.lx-term term="state-of-charge"} $e_t$ (MWh), with the gas plants, spill and the gap $g_t$ (demand minus nuclear, wind and sun) as in lesson 0:

$$\min \sum_t \big(40\,p_{\mathrm{cc},t} + 100\,p_{\mathrm{pk},t}\big)$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathrm{cc},t} + p_{\mathrm{pk},t} - s_t + d_t - c_t &= g_t && \text{(balance)}\\
e_t &= e_{t-1} + 0.8\,c_t - d_t, \quad e_{-1} = 0 && \text{(state of charge)}\\
0 \le c_t,\ d_t \le 25, \qquad 0 \le e_t &\le 100 && \text{(power and energy)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The state-of-charge rule is the only rule that links one hour to the next: it is what makes storage a problem over time. Here the whole loss sits on charging; many models split it, $\sqrt{0.8}$ each way. Charging and discharging in the same hour would only waste energy, so the solver never does it here.

Lesson 10 shows how to write such a model down, and lesson 11 how to check a solver's answer. Lessons A8 (how long should storage last?) and M3 (capacity expansion), both upcoming, choose the battery's size too.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>One day only. A battery's yearly value needs every day of the year, including days with no spilled sun (lesson A8, upcoming).</li>
<li>Perfect foresight: the solver knows the whole day in advance. Real operators schedule with forecasts that miss (lesson 4).</li>
<li>The cost of building the battery and of its wear, which would set a minimum spread worth cycling for (lesson 7).</li>
<li>The combined-cycle's ramp limit from lesson 0, and any limit on the wires.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="w9-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mw" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A 100 MWh battery can deliver 100 MW.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Its power rating sets how fast it can discharge: Prairie Town's 100 MWh battery delivers at most 25 MW, for four hours.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="make" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A battery adds energy to the grid.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It moves energy in time and loses some on the way: this one returns 80% of what goes in.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spread" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Buying at $40/MWh and selling at $45/MWh pays for this battery.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. 1 MWh bought for $40 returns 0.8 MWh, worth $36 at $45. It needs a selling price above $50.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="w9">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="earn" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 50 MW, 200 MWh battery with 80% round trip charges 100 MWh at $20/MWh and later sells all it stored at $60/MWh. What does it earn?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$4,000</li><li data-value="b">$2,800</li><li data-value="c">$4,800</li><li data-value="d">$2,000</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$2,800: it stores 80 MWh and sells them for 80 × $60 = $4,800, minus the $2,000 it paid.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dur" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">On 9 June 2025, going from a 4-hour to an 8-hour battery (both 25 MW) raises Prairie Town's saving by how much?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">It doubles</li><li data-value="b">About half again</li><li data-value="c">Only $96</li><li data-value="d">Nothing at all</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Only $96, from $7,240 to $7,336: there is no more spilled sun to store and no more peaker to replace on this day.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
